modeDesc.verbs: Conjugate common verbs in the past, present and future. Type in Arabic or in romanization (katabtu; macrons and dots are optional), or pick from four.
modeDesc.nouns: Pick the Arabic for an English word, read an Arabic word, or find its plural. Many plurals are “broken”: the vowels inside the word change (kitāb → kutub).
modeDesc.numbers: Numbers 1–100 in their counting forms. Type the Arabic or its romanization, or pick the digits.
modeDesc.sentences: Translate by tapping the Arabic words into order. Arabic runs right to left, so the first word goes on the right.
modeDesc.listening: Dictation: listen to a word or a sentence and type it, in Arabic or in romanization.

tableNotes.verbs: Pick a tense. Weak and irregular verbs are highlighted in blue. The root is the three consonants that related words share.
tableNotes.nouns: Singular, plural and the three-letter root. “Broken” plurals change the vowels inside the word.
tableNotes.adjectives: Adjectives follow the noun and agree with it in gender, number and definiteness. Plurals of things take the feminine singular.
tableNotes.prepositions: Most prepositions are separate words; bi- and li- are written joined to the next word.
tableNotes.conjunctions: wa- (and) and fa- (so) are written joined to the next word.
tableNotes.numbers: Counting forms, 1–100. Compound numbers say the unit first: wāḥid wa-ʿishrūn = “one and twenty”.

numberNotes.text: One and two follow the noun like adjectives (kitāb wāḥid) and are often left out: kitāb = a book; two books has its own ending, kitābān.
3–10 take the opposite gender of the noun they count: thalāthat kutub (books, masc.), thalāth banāt (girls, fem.). The noun is plural.
11–19 are two words, unit then ten: thalāthata ʿashar = “three-ten”. The counted noun is singular.
The tens end in -ūn: ʿishrūn, thalāthūn, arbaʿūn… The counted noun is singular.
Say the unit first, then wa- (and), then the ten: khamsa wa-ʿishrūn = “five and twenty”.
miʾa is also spelled مائة, with a silent alif, in many texts.

tenseOptions.label: Past
tenseOptions.title: Past (al-māḍī)
tenseOptions.description: Finished actions: katabtu = I wrote. Endings show the person: -tu I, -ta you (m.), -ti you (f.), -a he, -at she, -nā we, -tum you all, -ū they.

tenseOptions.label: Present
tenseOptions.title: Present (al-muḍāriʿ)
tenseOptions.description: Now or usually: aktubu = I write / I am writing. Prefixes show the person: a- I, ta- you or she, ya- he, na- we; -īna marks you (f.), -ūna you all and they.

tenseOptions.label: Future
tenseOptions.title: Future (sa- + present)
tenseOptions.description: Put sa- in front of the present: sa-aktubu = I will write. To say “will not”, use lan + the verb: lan aktuba.

functions.label: No “is” (nominal)
functions.description: In the present, Arabic has no verb “to be”: al-bayt kabīr = the house (is) big. A definite noun followed by an indefinite word makes a sentence. To negate it, use laysa (is not).

functions.label: Adjective agreement
functions.description: Adjectives come after the noun and match it in gender and in definiteness: bayt kabīr (a big house), al-bayt al-kabīr (the big house), sayyāra jadīda (a new car).

functions.label: X of Y (iḍāfa)
functions.description: Two nouns side by side mean “X of Y”: bayt aṭ-ṭālib = the student’s house. Only the second noun can take al-, and a final -a on the first is said -at: sayyārat al-muʿallim.

functions.label: Possessive endings
functions.description: Endings for “my, your, his…”: -ī my, -ka / -ki your, -hu his, -hā her, -nā our, -kum your (pl.), -hum their. kitābī = my book. A final -a becomes -at first: sayyāratī.

functions.label: Having (ʿinda)
functions.description: There is no verb “to have”. Use ʿinda (at, with) + an ending: ʿindī = I have, ʿindaka = you have, ʿindahum = they have.

functions.label: There is (hunāka)
functions.description: hunāka = there is / there are. Negative: laysa hunāka.

functions.label: Verb first
functions.description: Formal Arabic often puts the verb first: kataba aṭ-ṭālib ad-dars = the student wrote the lesson. A verb that comes first stays singular even with a plural subject: dhahaba al-awlād = the boys went.

functions.label: Wanting (urīdu)
functions.description: urīdu = I want / I’d like. Before another verb, add an: urīdu an adhhaba = I want to go.

functions.label: Likes (uḥibbu)
functions.description: uḥibbu = I like / I love. The thing you like takes al-: uḥibbu al-qahwa = I like coffee.

functions.label: Future (sa-)
functions.description: Put sa- in front of the present for the future: sa-adhhabu = I will go. For “will not”, use lan: lan adhhaba.

functions.label: Can (yumkinu)
functions.description: hal yumkinu an … ? = is it possible to … ? A polite way to ask for help.

sentenceTypes.label: Negative
sentenceTypes.description: Negated with lā (present), lam (past), lan (future) or laysa (sentences without a verb).

sentenceTypes.label: Question
sentenceTypes.description: A yes/no question starts with hal; others start with a question word.

sentenceTypes.label: Request / command
sentenceTypes.description: Asks for something or tells someone what to do.

progress.sourceNote: Rough guides only. Word-family targets follow vocabulary-size research (Nation, Laufer). Hours are scaled up from the European estimates: the US Foreign Service Institute puts Arabic in its hardest group for English speakers (about 2,200 class hours to professional level).

With an ending it means “have”: ʿindī = I have.
Written joined to the next word: bi-s-sayyāra = by car.
Written joined to the next word; li + al- = lil-: li-l-bayt.
amāma al-funduq = in front of the hotel.
bayna al-bank wa-l-madrasa = between the bank and the school.

conjunctions.note: Written joined to the next word: kitāb wa-qalam.
Written joined to the next word.
shāy aw qahwa? = tea or coffee?
Spelled with a small (dagger) alif: lākin.
Followed by a noun or a pronoun ending: li-anna-hu = because he…
idhā kāna ʿindaka waqt = if you have time.

letters.name: أَلِف
letters.tip: A single upright stroke. Usually the long vowel ā; at the start of a word it carries a short vowel. Never joins the letter after it.

letters.name: بَاء
letters.tip: One dot below. Like English b.

letters.name: تَاء
letters.tip: Two dots above. Like English t.

letters.name: ثَاء
letters.tip: Three dots above. th as in “think”, never as in “this”.

letters.name: نُون
letters.tip: One dot above, with a deeper bowl at the end of a word. Like English n.

letters.name: يَاء
letters.tip: Two dots below. A consonant y, or the long vowel ī after kasra.

letters.name: جِيم
letters.tip: A dot inside the bowl. Like j in “jam”.

letters.name: حَاء
letters.tip: No dot. A strong, breathy h from deep in the throat, like breathing on glasses to clean them.

letters.name: خَاء
letters.tip: One dot above. Like ch in Scottish “loch” or German “Bach”.

letters.name: دَال
letters.tip: Like English d. Never joins the letter after it.

letters.name: ذَال
letters.tip: dāl with a dot. th as in “this”. Never joins the letter after it.

letters.name: رَاء
letters.tip: Dips below the line. A tapped r, like in Spanish “pero”. Never joins the letter after it.

letters.name: زَاي
letters.tip: rāʾ with a dot. Like English z. Never joins the letter after it.

letters.name: وَاو
letters.tip: A consonant w, or the long vowel ū after ḍamma. Never joins the letter after it.

letters.name: سِين
letters.tip: Three small teeth. Like English s.

letters.name: شِين
letters.tip: sīn with three dots above. Like English sh.

letters.name: صَاد
letters.tip: Heavy s: pull the back of the tongue up. Vowels next to it sound darker.

letters.name: ضَاد
letters.tip: Heavy d. So typical of Arabic that it’s called “the language of ḍād”.

letters.name: طَاء
letters.tip: Heavy t.

letters.name: ظَاء
letters.tip: Heavy dh (as in “this”); many speakers say a heavy z.

letters.name: عَيْن
letters.tip: A voiced squeeze in the middle of the throat. No English equivalent: say “ah” while tightening your throat.

letters.name: غَيْن
letters.tip: ʿayn with a dot. A gargled sound, like a French r.

letters.name: فَاء
letters.tip: One dot above a small loop. Like English f.

letters.name: قَاف
letters.tip: Two dots above and a deep tail. A k made far back in the throat.

letters.name: كَاف
letters.tip: Like English k. At the start or in the middle it looks like كـ.

letters.name: لَام
letters.tip: Tall, with a hook below at the end of a word. Like English l.

letters.name: مِيم
letters.tip: A small round loop. Like English m.

letters.name: هَاء
letters.tip: A light h, as in “hat”. Its shape changes more than any other letter’s.

letters.name: هَمْزَة
letters.tip: The catch in “uh-oh”. Often sits on a seat: أ إ ؤ ئ. Not written in romanization at the start of a word.

letters.name: تَاء مَرْبُوطَة
letters.tip: Only at the end of a word, mostly feminine nouns. Said -a at the end of a phrase, -at when linked to the next word.

letters.name: أَلِف مَقْصُورَة
letters.tip: A yāʾ without dots, only at the end of a word. Sounds like alif: ā.

letters.name: لَام أَلِف
letters.tip: lām + alif always join into this one shape. Also the word for “no”.

marks.name: فَتْحَة
marks.en: fatḥa: a short a. A small stroke above the letter.

marks.name: كَسْرَة
marks.en: kasra: a short i. A small stroke below the letter.

marks.name: ضَمَّة
marks.en: ḍamma: a short u. A tiny wāw above the letter.

marks.name: سُكُون
marks.en: sukūn: no vowel. A small circle above; the letter closes the syllable.

marks.name: شَدَّة
marks.en: shadda: a doubled consonant. A small w-shape above; hold the sound twice as long.

marks.name: تَنْوِين فَتْح
marks.en: tanwīn fatḥ: a doubled fatḥa adds -an. The alif after it is silent.

marks.name: تَنْوِين كَسْر
marks.en: tanwīn kasr: a doubled kasra adds -in.

marks.name: تَنْوِين ضَمّ
marks.en: tanwīn ḍamm: a doubled ḍamma adds -un.

lessons.title: Dots make the difference
lessons.subtitle: ا ب ت ث ن ي and short vowels
goals: Read the five letters that share one shape: *ب ت ث ن ي*
Read the short vowels a, i, u and the no-vowel mark

steps.text: Arabic is written and read from right to left. The alphabet has 28 letters and no capital letters. Inside a word most letters join the next one, so a letter’s shape changes a little depending on whether it comes at the start, in the middle or at the end of a word.

Short vowels aren’t letters. They are small marks above or below a letter. Newspapers and street signs leave them out; beginners’ books include them, and so does this app. When you’re ready, turn off Vowel marks at the top of the page.
These five letters share one basic shape. Only the dots tell them apart: how many, and whether they sit above or below.

steps.note: One dot below. Like English b.
Two dots above. Like English t.
Three dots above. th as in “think”, never as in “this”.
One dot above, with a deeper, rounder bowl. Like English n.
Two dots below. A consonant y as in “yes”, or the long vowel ī.

steps.prompt: Which letter has three dots above?
steps.why: Three dots above is *ث* (th). Two dots above is *ت*, and one is *ن*.

steps.text: At the start or in the middle of a word, these letters shrink to a small tooth with dots, and only the dots tell them apart. At the end of a word they keep their full shape. The line ـ shows where a letter joins its neighbours; it isn’t a letter.

steps.title: ب in each position (read right to left)
The five letters at the start of a word

steps.note: A single upright stroke, usually the long vowel ā. Alif never joins the letter after it.
A small stroke above the letter.
A small stroke below the letter.
A tiny wāw above the letter.
A small circle above a letter means no vowel follows it. Here it closes the syllable: bat.

steps.why: The tiny wāw above the letter is ḍamma, a short u.

steps.text: A short vowel followed by the letter that matches it makes a long vowel: fatḥa + alif = ā, and kasra + yāʾ = ī. ḍamma + wāw = ū comes in the next lesson.

steps.label: ay and aw
steps.text: In *بَيْت* the yāʾ has a sukūn, so it doesn’t make a long ī. Fatḥa + yāʾ with sukūn sounds like “ay”: bayt. Fatḥa + wāw with sukūn is “aw”: *يَوْم* (yawm, day).

steps.why: kasra under the bāʾ, sukūn on the nūn: bint, “girl”.

lessons.title: Letters that stand apart
lessons.subtitle: ج ح خ د ذ ر ز و
goals: Tell *ج ح خ* apart, including the throat sound ḥ
Know the six letters that never join the next letter

steps.text: Like the dot family, these three share a shape: a hook with a bowl underneath.

steps.note: A dot inside the bowl. Like j in “jam”.
No dot. A strong, breathy h from deep in the throat, like breathing on glasses to clean them. Romanized ḥ, with a dot below.
One dot above. Like ch in Scottish “loch” or German “Bach”.

steps.prompt: Which letter makes the sound in “Bach”?

steps.text: Six letters join the letter before them but never the letter after: alif and the five below. After one of them, the next letter starts again in its starting shape. That’s why Arabic words have small gaps inside them.

steps.note: Like English d.
One dot above. th as in “this”.
Dips below the line. A tapped r, like the r in Spanish “pero”.
rāʾ with a dot. Like English z.
A consonant w, or the long vowel ū.

steps.title: The six letters that don’t join the next one

steps.prompt: In *وَرْد* (roses), how many letters join the letter after them?
steps.why: wāw, rāʾ and dāl are all non-joiners, so every letter in *وَرْد* stands on its own.

steps.text: ḍamma followed by wāw makes a long ū.

steps.why: One dot above is *خ* (kh). Then ḍamma, bāʾ with sukūn, and zāy: khubz, “bread”.

lessons.title: S, sh and the heavy letters
lessons.subtitle: س ش ص ض ط ظ
goals: Hear and say the four heavy (emphatic) letters
Read the dot under ṣ ḍ ṭ ẓ in romanization

steps.note: Three small teeth. Like English s.
sīn with three dots above. Like English sh.

steps.text: Four letters are “heavy” (emphatic) partners of lighter sounds. To say them, pull the back of your tongue up and back, as if starting to say “oo”. The vowels next to them sound darker: the a in *صَبَاح* is closer to the a in “father” than in “cat”.

steps.note: Heavy s.
Heavy d. Arabic is sometimes called “the language of ḍād”, because the sound is so rare elsewhere.
Heavy t.
Heavy dh (as in “this”). Many speakers say it as a heavy z.

steps.label: Romanization
steps.text: A dot under a Latin letter marks a heavy sound: ṣ ḍ ṭ ẓ. The ḥ of *ح* has the same dot but is a throat sound, not a heavy one.

steps.prompt: Which letter is the heavy s?

steps.why: Heavy ṭ, then kasra + yāʾ for a long ī: ṭabīb, “doctor”.

lessons.title: The last eight letters
lessons.subtitle: ع غ ف ق ك ل م ه
goals: Recognise hāʾ in all its shapes

steps.note: The hardest sound for English speakers: a tight squeeze in the middle of the throat, with the voice on. Romanized ʿ. Practise by saying “ah” while tightening your throat.
ʿayn with a dot. A gargled sound, like a French r.

steps.why: No dot: *ع* (ʿayn). With a dot it’s *غ* (gh).

steps.note: One dot above a small loop. Like English f.
Two dots above and a deeper tail. A k made far back in the throat.
Like English k. At the start or in the middle of a word it looks quite different: كـ.
Tall, with a hook below at the end of a word. Like English l.
A small round loop. Like English m.
A light h, as in “hat”. Its shape changes more than any other letter’s.

steps.label: Two h’s
steps.text: *ه* is a light h, as in “hat”. *ح* is the strong, breathy ḥ from the throat. Mixing them up changes the word.

steps.why: qāf, lām and mīm, with fatḥa on the first two: qalam, “pen”.

lessons.title: Hamza, tāʾ marbūṭa and doubled letters
lessons.subtitle: ء ة ى لا  ّ  ً
goals: Read hamza on its different seats
Say tāʾ marbūṭa and alif maqṣūra at the end of a word

steps.text: Hamza: the catch in the throat

steps.note: The catch in “uh-oh”. It often sits on a seat: alif, wāw or a dotless yāʾ. Romanized ʾ, and not written at all at the start of a word.

steps.text: Letters only found at the end

steps.note: Only at the end of a word, mostly on feminine nouns. It looks like hāʾ with two dots. At the end of a phrase it’s said -a; when the word is linked to the next one, -at.
A yāʾ without dots, only at the end of a word. It sounds like alif: ā.
lām followed by alif always join into this special shape. On its own it’s the word for “no”.

steps.prompt: How does *ة* sound at the end of *مَدِينَة* (city), said on its own?
steps.why: At the end of a phrase tāʾ marbūṭa is just -a. It becomes -at when the word is linked to the next one: *مَدِينَة الْقَاهِرَة* (the city of Cairo).

steps.note: A small w-shape above a letter means say it twice as long, as in “book-case”. Here: babba.
A doubled vowel mark adds -n. You’ll mostly see -an, written with an extra silent alif, in set phrases.

steps.why: The shadda doubles the lām: muʿallim, “teacher”.

lessons.title: Sun and moon letters
lessons.subtitle: al- (“the”) and how it’s said
goals: Know when the l of al- is silent

steps.text: Arabic has no word for “a”: *كِتَاب* is “a book”. For “the”, add *ال* (al-) to the front of the word, written joined to it.

Before 14 letters, the l of al- isn’t said. It merges into the next letter, which is doubled instead and gets a shadda. These are the sun letters, named after *الشَّمْس* (the sun). Before the other 14, the moon letters, you say the l, as in *الْقَمَر* (the moon).

steps.label: Tip
steps.text: Sun letters are all made with the tip of the tongue near the teeth, like t, d, s, n and l. The l would get in the way, so it merges.

steps.why: rāʾ is a sun letter, so the l merges into it. The shadda on the rāʾ shows that.
bāʾ is a moon letter: the l is said, and it carries a sukūn.

steps.text: That’s the whole alphabet. You can now read any word written with vowel marks. Practise in the Alphabet tab (Read words uses real words from the app), then try Nouns and Sentences. When reading feels easy, turn off Vowel marks at the top of the page and read the way Arabic speakers do, from memory and context.
